Why Physical Menus and Printed Zines Are Becoming Status Symbols

# Why Physical Menus and Printed Zines Are Becoming Status Symbols

**Dek:** In a culture where every reference is instantly available, paper has started doing the old work of a wristband, matchbook or tote bag. It proves you found your way into the room.

**Section:** While You’re Here  
**Category:** Taste

**Thesis:** Printed menus and independent zines have gained status because they carry evidence of access, judgment and human involvement. Their value comes less from price than from where they were found, who made them and how few people will encounter the same object.

**Why now:** Restaurants are recovering from their QR-code years, younger readers are treating magazines as collectibles, art-book fairs are expanding, and brands have begun producing zines to borrow the credibility of independent print.

---

The illustrated menus at Quo Vadis have a habit of leaving the restaurant.

Some are taken with permission. Others disappear more casually. Writer and artist Leanne Shapton once described slipping one of John Broadley’s menus into her handbag after dinner. It is easy to understand the impulse. Broadley’s drawings wander around the dishes in black ink: animals, faces, bits of scenery, people eating things they probably should not be eating. The date appears at the top, sometimes with the weather. The pie gets its own box.

Quo Vadis changes its menu daily, so the sheet in your hand has a built-in expiration date. Tomorrow’s version will look similar, though it will never be quite the same. The restaurant has been collaborating with Broadley since 2012, long enough for the menu to become one of its signatures, right alongside the smoked eel sandwich and Jeremy Lee’s fondness for suet.

Most menus are treated as equipment. They get wiped, reprinted or thrown away when the prices change. A Quo Vadis menu behaves more like a small edition from an artist who happens to work inside a restaurant.

It also gives the diner something to take home.

There is a modest economy forming around objects like this. Restaurant menus, zines, matchbooks, hotel stationery, event programs and oddly specific local publications are becoming the souvenirs of people who would rather not buy souvenirs. The object can be inexpensive or free. The important part is that it came from somewhere.

A printed menu from a difficult reservation says you got the table. A zine from an art-book fair says you knew the fair was happening. Neither has to announce much beyond that.

## Dinner begins with the menu

The pandemic briefly turned restaurant dining into a sequence of small technical chores. Scan the code. Approve the camera permission. Wait for the menu to load. Pinch the PDF until the appetizers become legible. Close the text that arrived while you were trying to decide between two pastas.
